utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A few things before I let Mr. Milovancevic continue with his cross-examination. On the housekeeping side, we are being offered, if we so wish, to sit tomorrow in the morning instead of in the afternoon, and also on the 6th. If people would like to have an early day being Friday, then we can sit in the morning tomorrow, and we can also sit in the morning on the 6th. Any comment, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, both of those dates are fine with the Prosecution -- or both of those changes would be fine with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a morning session tomorrow would considerably upset our rhythm of work that we envisaged. If it is not an absolute necessity, I would kindly ask Your Honour to keep the original schedule, that is that we sit tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that's next week. That's fine, Your Honour. As far as that day is concerned, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that other participants in the proceedings would also be comfortable with the change on the 6th. I'm talking mainly the interpreters and the other people. Would that be okay? If we sit tomorrow in the afternoon to accommodate Mr. Milovancevic, but in the morning on the 6th. Is that okay? Okay. I got a nod from the booth. We shall then sit, as scheduled, in the afternoon tomorrow and in the morning on the 6th. Okay. Thank you very much. There is an oral order or decision that we would like to make. This is a decision on the Prosecution's motion for testimony to be heard via videolink conference -- or video-conference link. I don't know. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion for testimony to be heard via video-conference link filed confidentially on the 3rd of February, 2006, in which the Prosecution requests that the testimony of protected witness MM-022, Witness MM-023, and Witness MM-040 be received via video-conference link pursuant to Rule 71 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence due to the ill health of the witnesses. The Defence did not file a response to the motion. On the 23rd of February, 2006, the Prosecution confidentially filed a notice of filing of medical information which contained medical certificates on the health condition of the witnesses. The Trial Chamber considers that the testimony of the witnesses concerns their involvement in specific incidents alleged in the indictment and therefore is sufficiently important to make it unfair to proceed without it. The Trial Chamber further considers that in light of the information provided in the medical certificates, the witnesses are unable to come to the Tribunal to testify in person. The Trial Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice that the witnesses testify via video-conference link and hereby orders that their testimony be given by means of video-conference link between Zagreb and the assigned courtroom at the seat of the Tribunal in The Hague in the week of 20th March 2006. The Trial Chamber further orders that the locations and exact dates of the video-conference link be determined after consultation among the parties, the Registry, and the Trial Chamber, taking into consideration in particular the health condition of the witnesses and the possibility to hear them in or around Zagreb. The Trial Chamber directs the Registrar to take all necessary measures in order to set up the video-conference link, including having regard to the protective measures for witness MM-022. Thank you. That is the end of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Before you start, Mr. Milovancevic, I think I must remind Mr. Babic. Once again, Mr. Babic, you have taken -- make a declaration at the beginning of your testimony. You are still bound by that declaration. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to continue your cross-examination today. As before, can we please go along with what the interpreters have asked us to do, that is to pause between question and answer so that there would be ample time to have everything interpreted. Last time, towards the end of your cross-examination, we spoke about the referendum on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia. That was in August, September 1990. And then we talked about the implementation of that decision, the adoption of the statute of the SAO Krajina in December 1990. Do you recall that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At this moment I would like to go back to something that you referred to in your testimony, namely your meeting with Mr. Martic in July 1990, on the occasion of the protests of the policemen from Knin. During your testimony, did you mention the petition that a group of policemen from Knin sent to the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, the secretary of the federal ministry in Belgrade, Petar Gracanin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I interpreting your statement correctly if I say that in that petition they expressed their opposition to the introduction of new Croat symbols in the police, that is to say new uniforms, a new name for their service, "redarstvenik," and also new emblems like the chessboard flag?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I remember that petition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many policemen signed this petition? Do you have any tentative figures, at least?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the majority of the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in July 1990 a meeting was held in Knin between the MUP of Croatia and the Knin police station. The aim of this meeting was for the policemen who signed the petition to turn obedient.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly what was said was, as presented by the members of the MUP, the police should do their job and not interfere in political matters. That is how they tried to get the conduct of the police in Knin in order, rather, the signatories of the petition. Petar Jurica; I've just remembered the name. I think that was the representative of the MUP from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were also present at that meeting. Why were you present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me because I was president of the Knin municipality, so I attended the meeting. Somebody called me. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at that meeting the policemen presented their reasons why they signed the petition, and the delegation from Zagreb presented their reasons, and basically everybody stuck to their original positions. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said a few moments ago, what the delegation of the MUP of Croatia asked for, and the policemen, on the other hand, expressed yet again what the petition contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In these talks, did the policemen give their reasons why they were opposed to the introduction of these changes in the police, why they were opposed to the new uniforms, the new emblems, and the new name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I cannot remember all the details, but I remember the general positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The new emblems, the new insignia for the police, did they make the police in Knin think of something? Were they reminiscent of something else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, symbols, uniforms, and the name of the police was reminiscent of, as they explained it - especially the name of the police; it is "redarstvenik" - it was all reminiscent of the police of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a name that was used during the Second World War, that is to say the Ustasha government in the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the name of -- that was the name of the police of that state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milovancevic please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this somehow coincide with the changes in the constitution of Croatia that were referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened in that period, yes, yes, after the Presidency of Croatia had this initiative to change the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we just remind everyone yet again what these changes were: That Serbs would no longer be a nation according to the Croatian constitution; that there would be a Croatisation, as you said; there would be a Croat emblem, Croat insignia, the Serbian language was being abolished, and regionalisation was being done away with.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the changes concerned. Yes, those were the changes involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You said that at one point there were quite a few people in front of the Knin police station. Do you remember how many there were, a lot, a little?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were masses there. The street was blocked? They heard that there were some members of special forces nearby. Why were they there? What were they supposed to achieve through their presence in front of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To give support to the police, to the policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In what sense? Were the policemen in danger due to the presence of the members of the special units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to express their solidarity with the demands of the policemen. I think that that was the main motive for this rally. And then information was received that there were members of special units in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Babic, that Martic was present at that meeting too, that the discussions of the Knin policemen were more or less the same, and that at one point you addressed the people gathered there, asking them to go home.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was towards the end, because the meeting did not yield any results. The delegation of the Croatian MUP got upset and a way had to be found for them to leave. It wasn't easy for them to get out, and that is why people were supposed to leave, so that they could leave the police station. That was why I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the people actually leave when you spoke to them or did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a few people spoke. I did. Other people did. People were still sticking around. It was all very slow and then, as far as I was told later, the delegation of the MUP of Croatia managed to leave through a back door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the accused Martic spoke at that time, but you remember that he gave some statements to the press, whereas now you say that this delegation left. Who saw the delegation off? Was it the policemen from the Knin police station that provided safe passage for them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just heard that policemen, probably, got them out of the station through some back door. That is what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Milan Martic's words, namely that as long as he is alive the Croatian chequerboard flag would not be on the fort of Knin, does that have anything to do with the departure of these guests from the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, it has a general meaning in view of all these events that were taking place. This had to do with the protest, the petition, the visit of the delegation, everything that happened in the conflicts between the MUP of Croatia and the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the Knin fort has a symbolic meaning, that this is an old fortress which is in the centre of town, that it constituted a strong -- an old military stronghold. It has to do with history and the past of the Serbs in the area and their fight against the Turks. Is that true, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is the statement of Milan Martic that as long as he is alive the Croatian chequerboard will not be flying at the Knin fort, did that express his opposition that a symbol from the Independent State of Croatia in which Serbs were victims should not be in a place which is holy in the history of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the Croatian state. The chequerboard represented the Croatian state, the new Croatian authorities; that was the symbol of the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 10th of August, 1990, briefly after the delegation from Zagreb came to the Split police station, you met with Milan Martic, that you were close to each other, and that Milan Martic came in a uniform to warn you that you were not safe. Is this correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think this was the 9th of August, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after this warning by Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arranged with his friend and associate Pepin Cupkovic for me to be urgently moved with my family to another building on the outskirts of Knin where we would spend the night. I was so disturbed by this that I accepted that proposal as something quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And was Mr. Martic disturbed? Was he convincing when he conveyed this warning to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, he was calm. He appeared to be calm, and calmly he said, "Everything is all right, but they're coming at us." His behaviour and his calmness was not quite in sync with what he was telling us and with what he was suggesting, for us to move, but he seemed calm and collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And why did you move? Was it because you felt insecure, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "They're coming at us," and he said that my security was under threat and that's why he said that I should move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you who was coming at us, who was threatening your security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian specials, the Croatian special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the next day David Rastovic, the vice-president of the Serbian National Council, and Bogoljub Popovic, vice-president of the SDS, told you that you should go to Milosevic to seek protection. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who were you supposed to seek protection for, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Serbs in Knin and in Krajina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was threatening the Serbs in Knin, Krajina, and Croatia, according to the information that you had? Who were they supposed to be protected from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two things, as I said. The Serbian National Council was scheduled -- after the Assembly in Srb, they decided to hold a referendum on Serbian autonomy. This was one event at that time to which the Croatian government responded that the referendum was illegal. The second problem which cropped up was the one created by the police officers in the police station by entering into conflict with the Croatian MUP. So there were two issues, open issues, or two conflicts on the scene. One was political, one relating to the referendum; and the second one, as the Croatian government was explaining it, was the uprising of the police in Knin. This is what was causing a possible intervention of the Croatian government and making them resolve issues by force, making the police officers behave by force and also to prevent the referendum from taking place by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This possible forceful intervention by the Croatian government, was that the reason why you went to see Mr. Milosevic, the then president of Serbia? You mentioned that he was at Kupari together with the president of the Presidency, Jovic, and you also said the federal minister for national defence was there, General Kadijevic. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were these two problems and we needed to seek protection from Milosevic in this matter. That was what was suggested to me and that was what I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that you also thought the same as those people who suggested that, that there was a danger of an intervention by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I accepted to relocate and to move to a different apartment, so that meant that I was upset myself, and I accepted the proposal because I believe that there was a realistic threat against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you sent a message via Mr. Vucetic to President Milosevic where you were seeking a meeting and whereby you were seeking protection and that Mr. Milosevic responded in turn that you should address the president of the Presidency, Mr. Jovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a sort of indirect conversation. It wasn't just an exchange of messages. Bogoljub Popovic and myself explained the problem to Vucetic, and he presented the problem to Milosevic, and he said all three of them were there, meaning Milosevic, Kadijevic, and Jovic [sic]. And as far as I understood, they discussed that question or, rather, the things that we talked about, and their response was that we should ask to be received by Jovic in Belgrade so that we could explain the matter to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that is what you did. So on the 13th of August, 1990, you were, at your request, received by the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Mr. Jovic, in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that that was when you discussed the political situation in Croatia, the constitutional changes made by the new Croatian authorities, also that you discussed that the Serbs in Croatia were planning a referendum and that the others discussed the threat of armed intervention by MUP of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. The gist of what I talked about dealt with the political issues and that the other two more -- focused more on the security issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Mr. Jovic, as president of the Presidency, in response to the information from you, stated that a draft law was being prepared on self-determination for the Assembly of Yugoslavia, that he supported your political struggle, and that the JNA, as a federal armed force, would be the guarantor for your political struggle, and it will be an instrument of support for your political struggle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after your conversation with Mr. Jovic on the 13th of August, 1990, you went to see the federal secretary for internal affairs, Petar Gracanin, and that he suggested that the referendum that you mentioned of the Serbs be held in accordance with the constitution of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Croatia. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not in the office of Mr. Gracanin. This was in the office of Mr. Jovic. This was one of the people from Jovic's cabinet who told us to which constitutional article we should refer to. We should use the constitutional article on self-determination, or determination, for the referendum. So this was before Gracanin -- before the meeting with Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you went to meet with Petar Gracanin to inform him about the situation and that you heard that after that, at a press conference, he stated that he had told you that you should erect barricades, but that was not actually like that, that he did not mention that in the conversation with you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he gave that statement to the press, but I also said that I do not recall whether he told us that at the time or not. I don't remember it. Perhaps he did say that when he received a delegation of the police officers from Knin. This is what I said. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the talks in Belgrade with the president of the Presidency in Yugoslavia, you returned to Krajina, and you said that on the 16th of August, 1990, there was a meeting at Dvor Na Uni where the Serbian National Council set the date for a referendum on autonomy by the Serbian people and that there was a meeting scheduled for that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the statement by the Serbian National Council on the referendum in August and September 1990 met with the opposition of the Croatian authorities and they announced that they would prevent that by force, and in connection with that you discussed several events in Knin on the 17th of August. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in your office, as the president of the municipality of Knin, on the 17th of August in the morning you received a telex from the president of the Obrovac municipality that Croatian special forces were attacking Obrovac and the region of Knin and they were also setting up barricades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I received a telex from Sergej Veselinovic in which he said that the Croatian special forces were crossing Mount Velebit towards Obrovac, that they were erecting barricades at Obrovac, whereas the information that Croatian armoured vehicles were entering Knin, this information I received from Dusan Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Croatian special forces arrived at Obrovac and if they tried to disarm the police station and the people who were assembled there prevented that on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that during those few days there was a concentration of weapons of the police reserve forces in one place. That's how the Croatian authorities termed that. I think that that happened on that day. I'm not sure. It could have happened on another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There are witnesses who did say that this was on that day when the gentleman you mentioned informed you about the events in Obrovac. Do you know what happened on that day on the 17th day of August in Benkovac? Did the special forces confiscate weapons in Benkovac? In Obrovac they tried and they didn't succeed. Did they succeed in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat this once again: Whether on that day or on those days --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I just object? I object to the form of the question which is, "There are witnesses that did say ..." I would object to vague references to other witnesses who have said something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was wondering, which witnesses are you referring to? Is there a witness who has testified on this point, and who is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. What I wanted to say was that there are witnesses who talk about that, but that will be a topic for another time. What I wanted to do now was just ask Mr. Babic whether he knew, as the president of the Serbian National Council and as president of the Knin municipality, that on the 17th of August Croatian special forces confiscated weapons from the reserve police in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said what I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Who are these witnesses? That's my question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are witnesses who live in Krajina and who will be testifying before the Tribunal when the Defence feels that the time is appropriate for the presentation of such evidence. I'm thinking of people from that area, people who are near Benkovac, Knin, and Obrovac. I'm thinking of the population of that territory. But right now I don't think that it is necessary to mention their names. If the Chamber believes that this question is not precise enough or that it should be reformulated, then I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Perhaps you would reformulate it along the following lines: That the Defence is going to lead evidence to the effect that the Defence has witnesses. You see, when you -- the way you formulated it earlier, it gave the impression that those witnesses you're referring to have already testified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the Defence has a witness who spoke about the fact that the Croatian police, on the 17th of August, tried to confiscate weapons from Obrovac and that the people assembled there prevented that while the Croatian police confiscated weapons from the reserve forces in Benkovac. You said that you didn't have any knowledge about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did have some information about the events that took place. I said that I wasn't sure whether it was exactly on the 17th or around that time, but there was a decision by the Croatian government and the MUP for the weapons of the police reserve forces, which happened to be in the police stations, should be collected and placed in other locations. So that was the reason why the Croatian MUP confiscated the weapons and moved them to different locations, which I -- I don't know what they were. So we are talking about the same event, but I don't know whether the event actually took place on the 17th in Benkovac. However, I do know about such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify the situation, on that day you mentioned a specific date, the 17th of August, 1990, when you received a telex from Obrovac and when Dusan Orlovic came and said that armoured vehicles were entering Knin. So in that time frame and in that context you are talking about the seizure of weapons from the police stations in that area by Croatian special forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about that time period, except the term used by the Serbs was "seizure" and the term used by the Croatia was "confiscation of weapons." So I hope now that that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I take the time during this little pause to say can we increase those little pauses in between your speeches, because I think we're going a little too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on at that day, on the 17th of August, on the eve of the referendum, Dusan Orlovic, who worked with Martic, came to see you and that he was very agitated and he said that Croatian APCs were entering Knin. That is his sentence that you quoted. And due to his anxiety, you believed that. You ordered a state of alert and then went to the village of Strmica. Who did you go with, and who was it that you ordered to be on -- in a state of alert?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told one of the officials to turn on the sirens in the municipality, and I went with a driver to Strmica. One of the drivers. I can't remember which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that on that occasion the situation that you described in Knin was such that a state of war was proclaimed, that this happened at the height of the tourist season, and that this echoed throughout Yugoslavia at the time. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that after a while you came to Golubic and you saw Martic and Orlovic there and that they said to you that there were no Croatian specialists there and that weapons were being handed out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that day, the 17th of August, helicopters with Croatian specialists that were flying to Knin were stopped by the JNA or, rather, the Yugoslav air force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that information in the newspapers a few days after that. On that day, I did not have that particular information. No one told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that on that occasion after the state of war was proclaimed weapons were being handed out to the reserve force. Is that not an obligation of the police in a situation when a state of war or a state of emergency is declared, that they call up the reserve force, hand out weapons, and provide security for all vital installations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons were handed out before the news on the state of war had arrived. Weapons had already been taken from the station before I arrived in Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told. It was loaded onto trucks. It had already been loaded that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Golubic a staff for roadblocks had been established and that this was on the basis of a decision by the Main Board of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were present at the meeting where this decision to establish a staff on roadblocks was established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the day after the 17th. It was on the 18th. I came to the meeting when the discussion about this started, but I went to another meeting, to Knin, so I was not there until the end of the meeting, and when I was there, when I learned about it, this staff had already been established, when I had learned of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did that decision make Mr. Martic the head of this project for barricades or, rather, the staff for barricades, roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the roadblocks consisted of and where they were placed, in which directions, which routes, and what was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roadblocks were placed around villages and Serb settlements in general, regardless of whether the village was on the outskirts of the municipality of Knin or some other Serb municipality or right in the middle of the municipality. So there were roadblocks everywhere on the roads: Between villages and the town of Knin, between one village and another village, between Serb villages and neighbouring Croat villages; So in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question: What did the roadblocks consist of? What were they made of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different ones. In some places they were real barriers, made of logs. That is why it was called the log revolution. And in other places these were piles of stones, and somewhere it wouldn't be anything but a bench on the road or some other symbolic obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the roadblocks were placed at all the roads that led to Serb settlements and that they were supposed to prevent uninvited persons from coming in or, rather, members of Croat special forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as a particular position is concerned, they were also supposed to prevent incursions by policemen and taking police stations. That is why the police did this. Or to have the referendum held, which is what people in villages did, as well as the SDS. So for the most part they were placed in order to prevent forceful takeovers of the police and the police station in Knin by the Croatian MUP. That was the police reason. And the reason of the SDS was the fact that the referendum was being organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say, quite briefly, that these -- when we say, quite briefly, that these roadblocks were used for self-defence exclusively?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that after the 17th of August, 1990, you came to Golubic, and that is a settlement near Knin, and you concluded that that was a military camp. That's what you called it, because there was an armed man guarding it. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a military camp not because there was one man there but because there were quite a few people there with weapons. The entire camp or part of the camp, as far as I could see, had a wire around it. It was far away from the centre. Say near the lake there was a barrier where the settlement was entered. So the entire settlement had become a military camp, in a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did all of this happen at the time when the Croatian special police was gathering weapons in the Krajina and in police stations, the way you described it? Was that that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that when Golubic became a camp that you suggested to Mr. Raskovic, president of the SDS, to have that camp in Golubic disbanded and that you think that it compromises the policy of the SDS, and that is indeed the kind of decision that was passed, and the camp was disbanded. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Mr. Martic honoured that decision because he left the centre in Golubic. Or, rather, the way you described it was that he went to another place but the staff in Golubic was disbanded. So that decision was carried through. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that for a while the staff remained there. They did not want to honour the decision.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that went on for a while until someone - I don't know whose good idea this was - someone thought of calling these people and giving them some alleged information to the effect that the camp would be bombed, and that is why Martic and the other people moved from the settlement first to the outskirts and then to a completely different village. Martic did not honour the decision on disbanding the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response -- in response to questions put by the Prosecutor, you said that after the decision to disband the camp that Martic first moved to a trailer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a while, but then I described what it was like. I described the time frame. Yes, a trailer on the outskirts of Golubic and then to the village of Oton, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these events that had to do with the referendum, the 19th of August until the 2nd of September, 1990 - that's the time frame - you mentioned a meeting on the 10th of September, 1990, and negotiations with the parliament of Croatia and the MUP of Croatia in order to see a calming down of the situation. Do you remember that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the referendum from the 19th of August until the 2nd of September was held at all and did the Serb people vote in favour of sovereignty of their own people within Croatia with an overwhelming majority?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was whether they were in favour of autonomy, and the question was answered by a yes; yes, they were in favour of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 10th of September, 1990, at the invitation of Jerko Vukas, who is a member of the HDZ, by the way, president of the municipality of Sinj, and you went to a meeting in order to resolve municipal problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that we resolved those questions earlier, Jerko Vukas and I, because we were presidents of neighbouring municipalities and because barricades that were between our municipalities, that had been placed by the Serbs, caused inter-municipal problems. So we resolved these problems. And then there was another question, since we had already been in contact, at Vukas's proposal and initiative, that I should meet with the other representatives of the Serbs from the area, with the representatives of the parliament and government. That was after the resolving of inter-municipal problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So at the initiative of Jerko Vukas, you agreed to go to attend a meeting with the representatives of the Croatian government and parliament, and you say that you saw Slavko Degoricija, president of one of the Chambers in parliament, and also the minister of the interior, Boljkovac. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who else attended the meeting with you, that is to say on your side, on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My proposal was or, rather, my request was the delegation -- that everyone should be accepted as the representatives of the Serb Council. Dusan Vjestica, Rastovic, and there were also officials from Donja Lapac municipality. However, since the delegation from Zagreb did not want to talk us to us in that capacity, then we agreed that we should be representatives of Serb municipalities. So these people, in addition to Vjestica, there was Rastovic who was president -- and then there was the president of the Executive Council of Lapac and the secretary of the municipality of Donja Lapac, Djukic, and I cannot remember the name of the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You had a meeting scheduled about political talks. Did you have a meeting of the Serb National Council? You were practically Prime Minister. You were president of the Executive Council. Did you have a meeting and did you say we are going to have meeting, I'm going to have a meeting, I'm going to have political talks with the top echelons of the Croatian government and the police? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Academician Raskovic and others were informed, and we did have a meeting of the Serb National Council in Srb right after these talks in Lapac. It's same municipality. And I informed Academician Raskovic, and the other members of the Serb National Council about these talks and then there was a discussion about the agreement that we had reached. There were those who were opposed to this but Academician Raskovic supported the agreement and we accepted the results of the agreement by a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any minutes from that meeting? Was this an official meeting of the Serb National Council or were these your internal discussions, discussions amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any minutes. I think that minutes were kept, but -- I think that there were minutes, but I don't have them. The minutes did exist, or, rather, I don't know where they are now. That would be an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The press release of the 10th of September on the talks with the delegation of Croatia, who signed it and who wrote it, actually?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press release? Well, the participants in the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What participants in the talks, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Degoricija, Boljkovac, Pecerski, I, Rastovic, Vjestica; there were several signatories. Roughly, it was both an agreement and a press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You as president of the Serb National Council are conducting political talks with the delegation of Croatia, and together with the delegation of Croatia you are giving a press release and the Croats are not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the delegation from Zagreb did not accept us in the capacity of representatives of the Serb National Council, and we represented the Serb municipalities. I was the representative of the municipality of Knin at that meeting, as agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And who was it that you agreed with to change your status from president of the Serb National Council to president of the municipality and to have talks in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not change my status. I was president of the municipality of Knin, and it was in that capacity that I was a member of the Serb National Council, precisely because I was president of the Knin municipality. As president of the municipality, I was elected to the Serb National Council. If you're asking me why I accepted the proposal and the request of the delegation from Zagreb to the effect that they want to talk to me only in the capacity of a representative of the municipalities, all of us as representatives of the municipalities, my answer can be because I wanted us to succeed, but my capacity and the capacity of all other negotiators was a valid and legitimate one by way of the elections. So in response to your question who authorised me, I was authorised through the elections when I was elected president of the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear Mr. Milovancevic's question. He overlapped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The weapons that were seized or, rather, that were taken from the police stations and that were distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the record, please, Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreter indicated that she hadn't heard your question because you overlapped. What was the question? And the answer to that question which is not recorded here is, "The weapons that were seized or, rather, that were taken from the police stations and that were distributed." What was the question to that answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This happened unwittingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said that in this status that you had, your agreement with Mr. Boljkovac and Mr. Degoricija was to return the weapons of the reserve force that the Serb police had distributed, but where? In which places? Where was this distributed? And then that a secretariat would be established by the Croatian government. Can you explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were taken in Knin and Donja Lapac, and perhaps some other municipalities. I wasn't sure at the time, but we were there at the negotiations, the representatives of the municipalities of Knin and Lapac, so we were in a position to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you agree with the Croatian government for it to return the weapons it had taken from the Serbian police stations or the police stations in the Serbian territories?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you what it was all about. The police stations were part of the Croatian Ministry of Internal Affairs. The weapons of the reserve police forces were in the warehouses of the police stations. For certain reasons known to them, the government of Croatia decided, and it announced its reasons why, it wished for the weapons, the weapons of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to take the weapons from the police stations and to place them at a different location. I can assume what their reasons were. They had an uprising in Knin. They had a police station that wanted to leave the system. This was in relation to Knin. I am not specifically sure about the situation in other municipalities. It was about taking weapons -- well, it wasn't about taking weapons from Serbian territory. It was taking weapons from police stations which had refused to be obedient to them any longer, and these were police stations in Obrovac and Donja Lapac. I think that was the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've answered sufficiently, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, excuse me. I've just remembered you asked me whether the -- whether Croatia returned some of the weapons to the Serb municipalities and so on. But in my previous answer, I explained how I understood the whole conflict to be between the police stations in Knin and Lapac and the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that in these conditions of the absence of trust on the part of the Serbian population towards the Croatian side and the changes in the constitution and the fact that they declared the referendum illegal and also at their attempts to disarm the police stations, in these conditions you, as the president of the municipality, were trying to agree to a restoration of the police stations under the authority of the Croatian authorities? And this wasn't a decision of any official body, this was something that you did on your own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing happened first, and that was that the Serbs were the first to take up arms. That is a fact. The second fact is that not Serbs but the police in Knin, Lapac, and other municipalities, Serb municipalities. Secondly, these police stations were part of the Croatian Ministry for Internal Affairs, and we were an integral part of the Republic of Croatia and we were conducting legitimate political discussions, debates, even disputes in order to seek a political solution for Croatia's future. We participated in the political process as legitimately elected representatives from municipalities, from the local authorities, together with the people from the Croatian Assembly and the Croatian authorities. So it was quite normal for us to seek a solution for the crisis which was escalating and which was threatening to escalate even more. This was something that was quite normal and natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were different views when you discussed this with Mr. Raskovic. Did he support you? You also explained that in Knin that evening when you issued the statement some people disagreed with your decision and they called you a traitor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Raskovic supported me, as the majority at the meeting of the Serbian National Council did. Jovo Raskovic at the time literally said shedding of blood was not something that suited us or the Croatian government. It was something that suited a third side, and it was implied that this third side was in Belgrade, and he told me, he explained what it was all about. And it was about the fact that somebody wanted unrest and disorder in Croatia and wanted to provoke an intervention by the JNA and to introduce military rule. That was the information about the possible development of events in Croatia. Myself and Raskovic agreed about this possible development of the situation, and that was our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, any normal person would be against such a development, but you say that a third entity had an interest there and you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'm going to object to that question. It's just that "any normal person." I don't know what's talking about, and I object to it. It's argumentative and improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rather suggestive of abnormality on the person addressed, Mr. Milovancevic. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Mr. Babic said he and Jovo Raskovic were against bloodshed and I confirmed that as a Defence counsel and said any normal man would be against bloodshed, and then I proceeded with my question. I can leave out the beginning of the sentence. If it's creating any kind of problem, I will just leave it out so that we avoid any kind of confusion. I do not want to be seen to address the witness in any -- in this manner, and I regret if it's taken in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You phrase the question without the initial part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Raskovic said that this suited a third party, and you also said that you believed that was someone in Belgrade. This is what you believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He explained what that would mean, and that's why I felt that that third party would be in Belgrade. He explained that somebody wanted bloodshed in order that the JNA would intervene and that military rule would be introduced in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I asked you so that was your conclusion that this was referring to Belgrade as an explanation for all of this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He told me exactly who would be carrying out the intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, have you heard of General Spegelj? You've already talked about that a number of times. I think that you did. Did you hear about his statement in October 1990, that each officer in Virovitica is covered by five armed men and that the principle of action would be you would approach them, fire into their belly, and nobody would be able to reach the barracks alive. This will not be a war, Mr. Spegelj said, this will be a civil war. There will be no mercy for women and children, the apartments would simply be shelled. Are you aware of this statement by Mr. Spegelj in October 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Martin Spegelj was the minister of defence in the government of the Republic of Croatia, and these words of his were played with film footage broadcast by Television Belgrade sometime in January, in late January 1991. I don't recall about the October time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Later, we will come back to this speech by Mr. Spegelj from October 1990 - I will show you a document - but now we're following the time frame that we started with. You said that the reaction to negotiations with the Croatian government was the opposition of certain people in Knin through the National Resistance Council, which issued bombastic statements, blew up the shops and apartments of Croats and Albanians with the aim of causing an intervention by the JNA in order for a state of emergency to be introduced and in order to remove the Croatian government and introduce military rule. Is that what you said, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that this was the policy of the president of Serbia, Milosevic, and Mr. Jovic, as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia; to occupy territories and to annex that area to the new Serbian state. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To set up a de facto situation, as Mr. Milosevic termed it, and to set up a territory where Serbs from Croatia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia would all live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said that this National Resistance Council emerged after September 1990, after negotiations with Croatian government representatives. And you also said that you saw Mr. Jovic, the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the 30th of August, 1990, and that he told you that he was in favour of political negotiations for the respect of the constitution of Croatia and Yugoslavia, and he even brought a person who explained to you how you could carry out the referendum. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as far as respect for the constitution of Yugoslavia, both Jovic and Milosevic were in favour of a firm federation, and they were in favour of the constitution, and they wanted to pass a law through the Assembly of Yugoslavia on the self-determination of people. What was your third remark?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what this right to the self-determination of people meant, which was supposed to be proposed or brought before the Assembly of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they publicly stated was a little bit different from what was de facto carried out in the field. Publicly it was planned to implement self-determination. Borisav Jovic explained, maybe on the 10th of September or around that time, he explained that on television. There would be a vote by the peoples of Yugoslavia regardless of the republican borders. So there was a possibility in that proposal, that was their position as well as their political goal which they were implementing later, that regardless of republican borders, a new state would be created out of the Serbs who lived in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw Mr. Jovic on the 13th of August, 1990, and that you met Mr. Milosevic for the first time in October 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had indirect talks with Mr. Milosevic on the 10th of August for the first time, and the first time that I met him face-to-face was in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So on what basis do you claim that the National Resistance Council was blowing up apartments, issuing bombastic statements, and causing unrest based on the instructions of Milosevic and Jovic and without you having seen Milosevic until October 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had information that unrest in Croatia and the causing of bloodshed was something that suited those in Belgrade, the third party, and that the JNA would carry out an intervention and set up military rule in Croatia. After that information and after what Mr. Martic and his people's police and armed people refused to return their weapons but escalated the conflict, then after Borislav Mikelic in Banija carried out similar things and caused an uprising and stepped up or escalated the situation, all I said was that this was the reason for these acts, so that the JNA would intervene and that military rule would be introduced in Croatia. That was the initial phase. It was a combination of Milosevic, Kadijevic. Up until March 1991 there were these attempts to introduce military rule in Croatia in different ways. That was just the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Other than Mr. Raskovic, for whom you said he gave you such information about the intentions of Belgrade, did anyone else provide such information to you about the intentions of Belgrade? Who else other than him told you about these intentions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I heard that in January. That was the next information that I received from Mile Grbic, from Bosanski Novi, who told me that the military was preparing something in Zagreb, some sort of coup d'etat, and that it would be a good idea to ask about this in Belgrade. After that, the people in Belgrade also told me, a man -- I think his name is Kalicanin, he was an officer in the information service of the JNA, that was approximately the name of his service. So this Kalicanin said that the JNA, the army, was preparing a coup d'etat in Croatia, that everyone would be replaced, including the government in Zagreb, even the presidents of the municipalities. After this information, Milosevic called me to his office and he told me that they -- or the JNA will be arresting Croatian ministers, that I was in danger, that I should not return to Knin but that I should live in Belgrade and that he would offer me protection. And he gave me public security service and state security service protection, and I stayed under his protection for 10 or 15 days, knowing or believing him that I was in danger because the army was about to arrest Croatian ministers and carry out a coup d'etat in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned. We will come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we mentioned the Council for People's Resistance. Do you know its full name? Is its full name the Council of People's Resistance Against the Oppression of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did mention the full name once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the composition of the council was never publicly announced, but you heard that some people were there, members of it Jovo Vitas, Neso Maric, and that Milan Martic was in it as well. How do you know? Were you a member of the council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know who was a member if you weren't among them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I saw those people. Secondly, I was told that they were issuing or taking announcements or statements on behalf of the council to Radio Knin. I would see them in front of the police station, and these were people who were around Milan Martic, who communicated with him. This was the group of people around him. They publicly declared themselves to be the Council of National Resistance. They never stated what the structure was within the body. I don't know whether it was just a public name or what -- if it was just another term for the people's police, as Martic described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever write the announcements of the council that were read out on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you used to see Jovo Vitas carrying the statements or the press releases, but that is also a person whom you claim threatened to kill you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would take the announcements of the council to Radio Knin, yes, and he did make threats against me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How can you know that he took these statements when you were on bad terms with those people? How did you know what he was carrying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told. Dusan Orlovic and Nebojsa Mandinic also took those announcements by the People's Resistance Council to Radio Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go and visit the Knin police station or any other police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to visit the Knin police station on a couple of occasions in my life; first when I was getting my personal ID card, and then later at this meeting in July that I talked about. I was there in April 1991, I think, when the press conferences began at the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, just to see what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the kind of weapons that a regular police station would have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard, I think Jovo Mitrovic was in charge of weapons there. He was some sort of person in charge of the storeroom. I had information about that. They had pistols, and they also had long-barrelled weapons. They had regular service pistols and long-barrelled weapons for emergency situations. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that none of the police stations, by establishment or by legal regulations, has dynamite on its premises?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what one -- a police station would have. What I said was that I saw Vitas bringing things out of the police station, and it was said that this was dynamite. I don't know whether this was something that a police station is supposed to have under the regulations or whether this was some sort of extraordinary situation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you watching from, and what did you see Jovo Vitas carrying that you took to be dynamite?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taking out some packages and placing them in his car, and I said, What is this? and somebody said, Jovo Vitas is carrying dynamite. Some of the people who were there told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you told us that the intentions of the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Borisav Jovic, and the president of Serbia, Milosevic, were to secretly cleanse some areas of Croatia and annex them to the territory of Yugoslavia, contrary to what was stated at certain meetings. And you also explained that you heard this from the late Jovan Raskovic, Professor Academician Jovan Raskovic. Or based -- actually, you came to that conclusion based on what he told you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you brought out a number of assertions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question to you. I'm sorry to interrupt. Is it correct that from conversations with a person you reached the conclusion about what the intentions of the Yugoslav political leadership were, and you concluded from a cafe owner in someplace in Banija that the Yugoslav political leadership was planning a coup d'etat and to replace the Croatian leadership? You heard that from a cafe owner. And you also heard from somebody that allegedly dynamite was being carried out from a Knin police station. You also said that you heard a number of other things from some other people. Do you know anything based on your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. This has now become about an eight-part question, and I would object on that basis. It's completely confusing. It's stitching together all sorts of different pieces. I think it's also mischaracterising the evidence that the witness has given, which has been a recurrent problem today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour. I'm going to put a very specific question, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have the leave if only you will put one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, your information about this, about the Yugoslav top leaders planning a military coup in Croatia and arrests in Croatia, did it come from a tavern owner in some small place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this information, and you did say that you heard from a tavern owner that arrests were being prepared in Croatia, was it on the basis of that that you went to Belgrade in January 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you no, and I keep saying no and -- could you please put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Mile Grbic? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned him in a series of events and contacts in terms of how I got information from President Milosevic about what was being prepared in Croatia. If you wish to hear more from me now in terms of what I know about Mile Grbic, then I can tell you, in addition to what I've already said, and that is that he is a man who had some contacts with General Andrija Raseta, one of the commanders of the Zagreb army district, and that he said to me that the army was preparing something in Belgrade and that it would be a good thing for me to ask around Belgrade to see what this was all about. So in connection with that statement of mine, you asked me now who Mile Grbic was. He's a man from Bosanski Novi where indeed he did have a tavern, and he had good connections with the army in the Zagreb army district and with Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have heard just now that you found out from a tavern owner that there would be a coup d'etat. Was that materialised as well as the arrest of the leadership of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I heard about a coup d'etat that would take place from a tavern owner, but I heard that he had information that the army in Croatia was getting ready for something and that it would be a good thing for me to get information what was in the making and what was being prepared in Belgrade. So my information in terms of what was being prepared for Croatia were from Belgrade. I told you. I mentioned two names to you. One of the two names is Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you say that in January you went to Belgrade, January 1991, after you talked to Mile Grbic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My trip to Belgrade after talking to Mile Grbic was not fully part of the sequence of events that I was talking about. It was one of the meetings. Mile Grbic sent me to ask around, to ask an officer from the military counter-intelligence service. Since you're asking me about Mile Grbic, he sent me to a particular man - I've forgotten the name of the officer in the meantime - to ask him what was going on in the military in Zagreb. Since this man did not give me an answer, he kept asking me about what was going on in the SDS, so this -- it's not that I got any information on the basis of these instructions from Mile Grbic. I got information based on other instructions from Boro Rasula, a friend of mine, a political scientist, later an advisor, a man who held high office in Belgrade and with good connections in Belgrade. He linked me up with Mr. Kalicanin, who was an officer from the information service of the JNA, who explained to me what it was that the army was preparing, and that was my next information, irrespective of this Grbic. And independently from this other information was the information about Milosevic, that they would arrest Croatian ministers. So they are going to remove the government or remove ministers, the way I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what did Mr. Milosevic say to you? Who is going to arrest Croatian ministers, he or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of an order of the Presidency of Yugoslavia from January 1991 that all weapons taken from the reserve force should be brought back and that the police should be brought into its regular framework?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order had to do with paramilitaries in general and all illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs from Krajina -- the Serbs from Knin specifically, that's what you could know about, did they return their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did partly. I don't know exactly what the quantity involved was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that period, did the Croatian government increase its police force several times, their "redarstvenici" as they called them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian government act in accordance with the order of the Presidency of Yugoslavia that all these extra policemen be disarmed and that they return their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got any precise information. The promise given was that Croatia would honour its commitment, and now the extent to which they did is something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the statement made by the Croatian government that they would not disarm their police on the orders of the Yugoslav Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the response of the Croatian government was, as I've already said. I think that some kind of agreement was reached between Mesic and Borisav Jovic. I think that they talked along those lines, that something would happen. As I said, I don't know exactly. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the conflict in Pakrac on the 1st and 2nd of March, 1991, in which the special police of Croatia intervened and when fire was first opened at the army. Do you know that on the occasion of that incident the Federal Secretariat of National Defence proposed to the Presidency of Yugoslavia that a state of emergency be imposed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was a pretext or not, I don't know, but a proposal to impose a state of emergency was sometime around mid-March. There was a discussion about that. Now, whether Pakrac was the reason for this or the pretext for this or something else, I don't know, but in my assessment it was a plan that had been prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I did not ask you about your assessments. I just asked you about what you heard and what you did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. It wasn't about Pakrac. I don't have information that this was due to Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion did the Presidency of Yugoslavia indeed impose a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the proposal made by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in mid-March 1991? Did the Presidency of Yugoslavia introduce a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the Croatian government refused to carry out a decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia to return the weapons of the reserve force of the police. The Presidency of Yugoslavia refused the proposal of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to introduce a state of emergency or martial law, and the story that you heard from this tavern owner about the disbanding of these forces and the return of weapons, that didn't really happen, Mr. Babic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear this story about the Croatian government from a tavern owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, again and again today I have -- I'm keeping a running list here, and I'm up to seven or eight. Defence counsel has mischaracterised what the witness has said either today or in his prior testimony. He will say, well, you testified this, and it's not quite exactly right. I can go through all the instances that have occurred today, but I don't think the Court needs to hear that. But it's just occurred again. The witness did not say anything about the Croatian government refused to carry out a decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia to return the weapons of the reserve forces of the police, and this tavern owner issue has been repeatedly addressed by the witness, and he has explained again and again what happened, and again Mr. Milovancevic is mischaracterising what the witness is saying. I would ask that if -- if the Defence counsel insists on characterising what the witness has said either today or in prior -- in his prior testimony, that he provide us, as is often done, with a reference, because I've been furiously looking through here, the prior transcripts, trying to match it up, and it doesn't match it up, and it would make it easier to follow if there was a reference. If he's not able to do that, I would ask that he simply put questions to the witness in whatever form he wants that's proper but not that he try to characterise what the witness has said beforehand because he continually makes mistakes in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course the Defence is not going to put questions that suit the Prosecutor. It's precisely questions that do not suit the Prosecutor that the Defence is going to put. What I'm trying to check is whether this witness is telling the truth when he is under oath, whether he's telling the Court the truth, and now we have reached a situation where I am trying to get an explanation from the witness. I'm not trying to put words into his mouth. I'm not trying say that he said something he did not say. I'm just pointing out things that are illogical that make his testimony totally senseless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you say that you are not putting words into the mouth of the witness. The objection is precisely that, that you keep characterising his evidence and mischaracterising it, for that matter. You are perfectly entitled to put questions. You are not entitled to mischaracterise or embellish the evidence of the witness. A very recent example is the last time the witness answered you.
