He said very emphatically, "I have not said to you that I heard about this information from the owner of the tavern," which is proof, if you are listening to what I'm saying. Mr. Milovancevic, it would be appreciated if you -- I'm talking. It would be appreciated if, when I'm talking, you want to listen to your co-counsel, you ask that I stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, indeed that objection is upheld, and I'm asking you once again don't misquote the witness. Put your questions to him. If you have to quote the witness or you have to refer to what the witness said, give us a reference. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said that you went in January 1991, that you went to Belgrade and that then you were provided with security because you were told that you were in danger. Who was it that endangered you and what kind of security detail did you get?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called to Milosevic's office, and Milosevic said to me that Croatian ministers would be arrested, that the JNA would arrest Croatian ministers, and that I was in danger in Knin. I was endangered by the Croatian government because they were expecting resistance and that that is why I have to stay in Belgrade under his protection. He sent me to the Ministry of the Interior or, as it was then called, the secretariat. He sent me to see Radmilo Bogdanovic so that he would provide this protection for me. Before that, he asked me where I lived or, rather, he offered me to stay at the residence of the government of Serbia in the so-called Boticeva villa. Since I said to him that I'm staying with relatives, then he said that I should tell Radmilo Bogdanovic that and that I should stay in Belgrade under the protection of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia until he told me that I could leave Belgrade. After that meeting I had with him, I went to Bogdanovic's office. He asked where I was staying, and he provided protection from the public security, that is to say the police, the Belgrade police. He also sent me - Bogdanovic did - to Jovica Stanisic, one of the state security officials of Serbia. And Jovica Stanisic provided me with security or, rather, an escort from the state security. These were civilian -- these were people in civilian clothing who would follow me in a car wherever I went anywhere around Belgrade. So they followed me all the time; when I was staying at home and when I was moving about town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did that mean, Mr. Babic, that that police that protected you protected you from danger that was coming to you from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Milosevic explained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that after about 20 days you received information that people were saying in Knin that you left the -- that you left Knin for the third time, that the population was on their own, and that it would be time for you to return.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say -- well, yes. I said that people were talking around town in Knin that I had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering if we could have the reference from counsel. He said, "You explained ..." If he could give us a reference where that is in the testimony. I'm not disputing that that's what he said in this instance. I don't -- it's just easier to follow if we could have the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Martic -- or, rather, Mr. Babic explained that when he received information from Mr. Martic, he first left Knin on the 10th of August, 1990, then the second time on the 18th of August, 1990, and then in January 1991, every time fleeing from the Croatian authorities because he was in danger. I just put all of this together, all this information that Mr. Babic presented here when replying to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true that I said that. It's not true that I said that I was fleeing from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please talk. Sorry, Mr. Babic. I'm sorry. Counsel is still talking to me. Mr. Milovancevic, the request to you is very simple. It is not disputed that the witness may have said what you say he said. You are just being asked to give a reference. Please give a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honours. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You might perhaps want to check on the transcript of the 17th of February, 2006, at T1522 to 23. Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have heard you. Just one moment, please. Your Honour, 1522, line 22, it says: "At one moment I decided to go back to Knin because there were rumours to the effect that I had fled." As for that part of the text, I interpreted it to the witness. I was speaking freely, without putting anything to the witness that he had not said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is precisely the problem, that the counsel is so-called interpreting what the witness has said. And in that last little speech that the witness tried to respond to where he said the witness -- Mr. Babic explained that when he received -- that each time when he left Knin - it's about to disappear from my screen - on the 10th of August, 1990, 18th of August, he was fleeing the Croatian authorities because he was in danger. That on no interpretation is what the witness has said, and -- and it is for this reason that I would ask from now on if the -- if counsel is going to try to interpret or try to quote what the witness is saying or has testified to, that he in the question provide a reference so that it can be checked. Otherwise, that he find a different way to put the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just check this. Mr. Babic, is it correct that you left Knin three times for Belgrade and each time you were accused of fleeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now you may proceed and ask questions, Mr. Milovancevic. We've asked the question without referring to the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've said that in January or late January, about 20 days of staying in Belgrade, you came back to Knin because of rumours that you had left Knin. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned because Radmilo Bogdanovic told me to return to my people. Along with that I also mentioned that there were rumours in Knin that I had fled. I wasn't there for a long time. I returned because Radmilo Bogdanovic permitted me to return or, rather, Milosevic, because I assume that Radmilo Bogdanovic had Milosevic's permission, because Milosevic told me I mustn't leave Belgrade, that I shouldn't leave Belgrade until he allowed me to do so. I said that I was constantly surrounded by Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did you return to Knin after that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We talked about the events of the 17th of August, 1990. Do you know anything about the 21st of August, 1990, when the Croatian forces approached Knin from two sides? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure about the date, but it's approximately around that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian police, from the direction of Sibenik and from the direction of Split, a few days after the 17th of August, set out towards Knin. They were stopped at the barricades at Klanac between Drnis and Knin, and at the barricades at Civljani between Knin and Sinj. These are the incidents that I know about, and I think from your question these are probably the incidents that you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Babic. After the referendum on the autonomy of the Serbian people, which was held on the 19th of September, 1990, until the 2nd of September, 1990, the SAO Krajina was declared. Could you please tell us what this decision was linked with. Was it linked with any kind of Croatian decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first declaration of the SAO Krajina, almost a month after the referendum -- the referendum results were proclaimed on the 30th of September and that's when autonomy was proclaimed. Nothing was done to institutionalise this decision until the new change of the Croatian constitution. In the autumn, in October, November and December, there was a public discussion about the adoption of a new constitution for the Republic of Croatia. One of the proposals for new constitutional norms was to form an autonomous district according to the Croatian model. The new constitution, the new draft constitution of Croatia, provided for the creation of a -- of regions, so-called "zupanjas." And as part of that discussion I suggested that one zupanja, one district, be called Serbian Autonomous Region, or Zupanja Krajina. Since Vladimir Seks, the president of the Assembly commission already rejected this proposal with derision, the proposal was made in the form of a draft for the statute of the Krajina. So it was quite specific. And since the proposal was rejected already during the debate, the Serbian National Council made a draft proposal of the statute to the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika so that that association of municipalities, which to date existed as a region, would be constituted in a new way as the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, which was actually something that was implemented on the 21st of December. This was two or three days before the adoption of the new Croatian constitution. And this was done for a sort of legalistic reason, in order to maintain this association of municipalities before the change of the Croat constitution went into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Could we say that the creation of the SAO Krajina as an autonomous region within Croatia was the response of the Serbian people to the changes in the Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just a response. It was something that was the preservation of -- it was an achievement, and the achievement was the association of municipalities as a self-governing regional body. So it was a form of a response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs ejected from the constitution of December 1990? Was regionalisation banned, and was the Serbian language banned, and were new symbols introduced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we cannot speak about them being ejected from the new constitution. We could say that they were ejected from the old constitution, because in the old one there was the possibility of regionalisation. In the old constitution this was something that was provided for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the statute of the SAO Krajina from December 1990, the SAO Krajina had an Executive Council. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you the president of the Executive Council, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the Provisional Executive Council, and I was the president of that Provisional Executive Council of the SAO Krajina dating from December 1990 until the end of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This Provisional Executive Council of SAO Krajina, on the 4th of January, 1991, did it make a decision, adopt a decision on the formation of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the same date when the decision was adopted to create the secretariat of SAO Krajina, was Milan Martic appointed the secretary of the SUP Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was elected to the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We saw that decision as evidence under Rule 65 ter. It's Exhibit 46. It's -- these are the minutes of the 4th of January of the session of the Executive Council, which noted that the decision was adopted unanimously and that the proposal that Martic be appointed as secretary of the SUP was also adopted unanimously. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was adopted unanimously, and the proposal was made by Rastovic, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that as the president of the Provisional Executive Council, you voted for this decision because the majority was in favour and because it was profitable for you. That is what you said. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it wasn't wise or profitable for me to oppose the decision because I did not have a counter-proposal, and the candidate was very well -- a very well-known public figure. So my opposition, without a better candidate at that point in time, would not suit me politically. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 183 of the Prosecution showed the Chamber the telex message that the Executive Board of the SAO Krajina sent on the 5th of January, 1991, to the federal bodies, the republican bodies, about the establishment of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs of the SAO Krajina. Are you familiar with such a decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true or is it correct that this message was sent to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, to the federal SUP, to the Ministries of the Internal Affairs of Croatia, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as to the political administrations or, actually, to certain police administrations in Croatia? Do you recall that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you explained that on the 19th of January, 1991, after the SUP was established, a regulation was adopted about the internal organisation and the operation of the SAO Krajina SUP? This was done by the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was Exhibit 646 under the 65 ter list, and it was introduced into evidence as Exhibit 184. You explained that this organisation was in force until the 1st of August, 1991, when the decision was adopted to implement the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under Exhibit 185, a document was introduced from the 65 ter exhibit list under number 1849. That was the Law on Internal Affairs from July 1991, in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, and the decision on its implementations on the territory of Krajina. We talked about that a little bit earlier. This is not in dispute; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that on the 1st of August, 1991, a decision was adopted on the implementation of a whole series of Serbian regulations on the territory of the SAO Krajina. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a whole series, but that day what was adopted was the decision to implement the Law on Defence and the decision to abolish the state security service in the territory of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You explained that on the 29th of August -- of May, 1991, in Krajina, Mr. Martic was elected as Defence Minister. This is 65 ter Exhibit number 79. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that on the 29th of May, 1991, the government of the SAO Krajina was formed, that you became the president or the Prime Minister of that government, and that the -- instead of the Secretariat, the Ministry of Internal Affairs was introduced, as well as other ministries. Is this correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Mr. Martic carried out the offices of the Defence Minister for only two or three days. That is how long he remained at that post, and formally until the 27th of June, 1991. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The reason why you proposed Mr. Martic as minister of defence was that you wanted to weaken his power, because he was controlling the MUP, the special forces, and he was neglecting public law and order. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that Mr. Martic was appointed minister of defence on the 29th of May, 1991, by the Assembly at the proposal of the government. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at my proposal, at my initiative. The government was just being constituted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the SAO Krajina Assembly on the 27th of June, 1991 - this is 65 ter Exhibit number 34 - adopted a decision on the election of Milan Martic as minister of MUP and that Martic remained at that post until early 1994. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that from the 27th of June, 1991, you were carrying out the duties of defence minister instead of Martic. Is this correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not instead of Martic, but since that ministry post was not filled, I, as president of the government, was performing the duties of defence minister until the election of a new minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why the decision was adopted to apply the Law of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of Krajina? What was the practical reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic was the one who proposed the adoption of such a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Babic, that the government of the Republic of Croatia, on the 21st of February, 1991, adopted a decision on the cessation of the laws of the Republic of Yugoslavia on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to leave Yugoslavia was adopted, but I don't know whether it was at that point all the laws of Yugoslavia ceased to be in effect, because Croatia adopted its declaration of independence in June 1991. So between that -- those two dates there was a sort of situation in force in accordance with that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the SAO Krajina, in late February 1991, adopted a decision to leave Croatia because Croatia had adopted a decision to leave Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Can I hear the question again? You're saying: "Do you know that the SAO Krajina, in late February 1991, adopted a decision to leave Croatia because Croatia had adopted a decision to leave Yugoslavia." Is that what you said? To leave Croatia or to leave Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It was a decision -- I asked the witness if he knew about the decision of the SAO Krajina to leave Croatia, because in late February Croatia adopted a decision to leave Yugoslavia. And it also adopted a decision whereby the laws of Yugoslavia would cease to be in effect in the territory of Croatia. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did you explain that in December 1991, in Krajina, you adopted your own law on the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and that you did that upon the recommendation of President Milosevic, the President of Serbia, so that the open links with Serbia would not be so evident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said two things. I think these were two separate questions. In December, yes, the law was adopted on -- the Law on Internal Affairs of SAO Krajina was adopted, while -- if I remember correctly, I think that was maybe a question relating to Milosevic's suggestion to adopt laws in SAO Krajina by copying the laws of the Republic of Serbia instead of directly implementing the laws of Serbia so this direct link would not be so evident. And this question and answer relating to the Ministry for Internal Affairs is one thing, but this suggestion from Milosevic dated from an earlier time, from early summer when we began to implement Serbian laws in the territory of Krajina. And this also included the Law on the Ministry of Internal Affairs. But there were other laws as well. So this recommendation of his was one of a general nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what the wording of his recommendation was so that we can distinguish between what your understanding is and what he actually said. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we should not promulgate the laws of Serbia but that we should simply copy them and then carry them out. It boils down to the same thing, but you don't see the direct link with Serbia that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, had Croatia already reached its own decision on federal regulations becoming null and void in its territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this recommendation of Mr. Milosevic that you referred to, you said that the public strategy was to preserve a strong federation - that is what was advocated publicly - and that the secret strategy was the establishment of paramilitaries in Croatia, the provoking of incidents and provoking an intervention by the JNA so that these new territories could be annexed easily. Is that the way you meant it? I think I've roughly managed to summarise your words.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be a summary of the political objective that Milosevic advocated from the summer of 1990 until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a witness in the trial of the accused Mr. Milosevic, and did he deny that claim, and did he put questions to you to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness. The testimony went on for a long time. What's your specific question that I'm supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do, Mr. Babic. You said that somehow parallel to Martic's appointment as minister of national defence you passed a law on abolishing the state security service in the territory of the Krajina. Do you remember that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention the decision dated the 1st of August, 1991? That is Prosecution Exhibit 187, document 106 from the 65 ter list of documents. So it was published in the Official Gazette, and in paragraph 2 it says that the government should present a proposal to establish a governmental agency for national security. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the arrangements at that time, did the Secretariat of the Interior have two services, the public security service and the state security service? So it was under the Ministry of the Interior until then. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that, according to this decision of yours to abolish state security, and the decision is dated the 1st of August, 1991, the objective was to adopt a European solution, to have a government agency for national security independent of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was to take power away from the state security service, and it consisted of the state security service of Serbia and the state security service of the SAO Krajina, and that is why the decision says that the state security service is abolished in the territory of the SAO Krajina. That's the wording, not abolishing the state security in the Secretariat or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina. So the objective was to free the Ministry of the Interior of the DB of Serbia, the state security of Serbia, and the state security of Krajina in a way to have Martic placed under the control of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I am right -- am I right if I say, Mr. Babic, that you passed this decision with that objective in mind on the 1st of August, 1991? That was when the decision was reached; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you state that after the events in Plitvice in April 1991 you sought technical and other professional assistance from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I sent a letter. Well, to remind Milosevic of his promise given in March, that is to say to carry through the previously made promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the essence of this request from April? What kind of assistance did you need? What kind of assistance and what for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said what Milosevic had promised. Two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, sorry. I didn't ask you that. I asked you something different.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was your objective? Tell us that first, and then you can tell us what it was that Milosevic said to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in April I sent a letter in order to remind Milosevic of the promise made, to have this promise carried out. I wanted to say what the promise was, I wanted to say what the message from this letter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point of what Milosevic promised was that he would give professional assistance to organise the Secretariat of the Interior of the SAO Krajina, and he said that he would arm the Krajina or, rather, that the arming of Krajina had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you were in Belgrade as a representative of the Knin authorities after January 1991? When in March and April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On these occasions did you ask the Republic of Serbia for protection from what the Croatian authorities were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in March a question was put to Milosevic how he intends to protect us under these new circumstances when the Presidency did not pass a decision on the engagement of the JNA. That was the reason for putting that question. So an answer to your question is along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So is it correct that you were concerned or perhaps even afraid due to the decision of the Presidency not to introduce martial law? You took this as a warning; am I mistaken or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic's next political objective was for the Serbs of Croatia to have the right to remain in Yugoslavia. So we passed this decision on disassociation from Croatia and practically we severed all communications and ties with Croatia in terms of seeking any kind of solution. Milosevic had already brought us into that situation. And after that the question was who would protect us then when we were in that position politically, because, as we had already seen what the situation was, his guarantee that it would be the JNA that would protect us was no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said to us during the course of this day that in August 1991 you addressed Jovic and then later on in 1990 Milosevic for the first time and that you had meetings, and that you told them about your fears from the Croatian authorities, that you sought the support of federal authorities. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, meetings were held when Milosevic would send a message for us to come. I went, Academician Raskovic went, other people went with me, or he'd ask us to make a public request to him to have him receive us, as was the case in January, and then we would go to see him. Regardless of what we talked about, he always presented it as the Serbs coming due to their fears, seeking protection, that's how it was portrayed by his side most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in Pakrac on the 1st and 2nd of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that, what I heard from the media. I can repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. Babic. We've already heard that. Thank you. So you don't know anything specifically. You have no direct knowledge as to what happened there, only what you heard and read.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what Milosevic said to me about that, that I should not worry about what was going on, that I should go to Knin in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Dzakula appeared before this Court, who is from the area and who explained that on that day the Croatian special police intervened and that there was an armed conflict and the JNA intervened and that the Croatian special police first opened gunfire at the JNA on that occasion. Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the media. That's what I said, that I heard that the situation there was very dramatic, and that Bosanac got killed, and that turned out to be false. Well, that's what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might raise an issue here that's come up, and there's a bit of a cultural difference here perhaps. In my practice, in my -- back home, it's not proper to put to a witness what another witness has said, either in testimony or in a witness statement. The fact that is contained in the witness statement or in the testimony can be put to the witness but not in that form. That is: Witness X testified this way, what do you say about that? That's my practice, that it's -- that that is not permissible. I know that in this building it's gone both ways. It's -- sometimes that's permitted and in other cases it's not permitted. I think there are very good reasons not to do that, because I think in -- the witness should be testifying from his or her own knowledge even if confronted with facts and confronted on cross-examination with leading questions, that's fine, but should not be -- for me, I think that it can be -- it can be improperly influential or distracting or a problem if the witness is confronted with the fact that another witness said this or -- that is just my view of the matter and perhaps the Court could give us some guidance on that, what its view is on whether these sorts of questions are proper or not. I don't think that -- in my view, it doesn't add anything to the question, and it's -- it's possibly distracting or in some cases it might influence a witness improperly. Because it's a natural reaction when you're testifying, when you hear somebody else said something, it can be -- I think it can be unduly influential. I'm not saying it's -- that's the case here, I'm not saying that's what happened, I just thought it was an appropriate time to raise it because I'm aware that this is an issue in the building and I thought perhaps the Court could give us some guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any authority on -- or a basis for this -- for raising the issue? What is the authority for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just relying on my -- on practice in my national jurisdiction, which I don't have an authority at hand for that. And I'm also aware that in -- in the last trial that I did, in the Limaj trial, it was -- it kind of went both ways. There were some counsel that thought it was okay to do that and it was done sometimes. There were other counsel who did not think that that was a proper way to ask questions. And I know that in other cases -- I believe in the Brdjanin case those sorts of questions were not permitted; that you could not say that, "This witness said this, what do you say about that?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your first address has now disappeared from my screen. I wanted to quote it to you because I actually don't understand what you are saying, but let me try and paraphrase you. I thought you said -- I cannot -- you said that the fact that the statement was made or the testimony was given can be put to the witness but not in that form. Not in which form?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have been more clear. What I meant is that in my practice it's okay to say -- it's okay to put the question in this form: "Isn't it a fact that Croatian police officers fired first on that occasion?" That question would be permissible. It would not be permissible to say: "Witness X testified here ..." or "Witness X said in a statement that Croatian police officers fired first on that occasion. What do you say about that?" Or "Isn't that true? " So the fact that it's been testified to or that it's in the statement can be put to the witness in a leading form or a non-leading form. That is perfectly proper, I think. But to add to that that a witness has testified to that, whether the witness is identified or not, that -- that, I think, is improper. I don't think it adds anything, and I think it's improper. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm still struggling to find the impropriety of the question, because -- I'm trying to find out what would be wrong to say, "Somebody said this, do you have any comment?" And your comment could be, "I agree with somebody," or "I disagree," or "I have no knowledge." I'm not sure how you say it influences improperly --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The rationale in the practice where I come from for not allowing that sort of question is that -- is that it -- is that it -- it adds a certain weight to the question that may have some effect on the witness. And again, I'm not saying that that's the case here. I'm not particularly concerned about that. But in -- with respect to other witnesses, if they hear, oh, well, another witness has said that, or several other witnesses have said that, that could -- I think that's -- the rationale is that that's distracting, that it could have undue influence on the witness. I'm only putting to you the practice that I'm used to. And I don't particularly see what it adds to the question to say that another witness has testified to this. If you're putting -- the important thing is to put the fact to the witness and get the witness's testimony. To say that another witness has testified to this or will testify to this, which of course is -- adds the element of speculation, I don't think that adds anything to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. I would just like to respond briefly, Your Honours. My question referred to the statement of a very influential political figure from Pakrac. The witness who is here knows that person very well. He knows his political role, and he's informed about it. It was my intention to present to the witness the contents and the seriousness of the information that a certain witness - and in this case it was this specific witness - but I don't see what the difference in cultural terms that the Prosecution mentioned could be the reason not to put a question like this. What we're talking about here is whether something is well-grounded or not, whether something is permissible and whether it's in accordance with the practice before this Tribunal or before other institutions. A question put in this way, to me, absolutely seems to be unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand that last sentence. To be unacceptable or acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection unacceptable, Your Honour, because cultural milieu differences cannot be the grounds to put impermissible questions. I am putting a legal question or a proper question or not, but the way the Prosecutor is presenting the matter I think is groundless and it's not really serious. I would also like to draw your attention, Your Honours, to the fact that perhaps this is a good moment to go on a break, if I am not mistaken. I am watching the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are right. Let's do so and maybe let's deal with this objection when we come back. We will reconvene at quarter to six. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we have had opportunity to look at the transcript, and the transcript says -- it doesn't say, can you comment on this. It says, have you heard of this. Would that make it still objectionable?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I mean, the answer to your question is yes. I'm sorry. I don't think that that -- that phrase -- phrasing necessarily makes a difference. The objection is rooted in the fact that the witness is being confronted with the statement or testimony of another witness. And if I could just add briefly two points. I know -- I know I wasn't invited to do so by the Chamber but if I could just briefly add two points because I had an opportunity, over the break, to reflect a little further bit on this. The first point is that an additional reason that this practice is followed in my jurisdiction - that is you're not allowed to confront with the testimony of another witness in that way - is that it invites witnesses to comment on the credibility of other witnesses, which is -- which invades, in a sense, the province of the Court. That is up to the Court to decide credibility issues, and therefore that's another reason that it's considered improper. The other point that I would make is there may be on this issue a distinction between confronting a witness with the testimony of a witness who has actually testified in the trial, who has come here and testified and has been cross-examined, testified under oath, and confronting a witness with a witness statement or a declaration that has been made to one of the parties but who has not come and testified at the trial. That may be another distinction that the Court may wish to entertain, and it may be -- it may be proper to confront with witnesses who have testified at the trial but not in the case of witnesses who have made statements but who have not testified. And that's -- that distinction would be based on a different reason than what I have articulated as a basis for the objection, but I just throw it out there as something that the Court may want to consider. Finally, I would just say that I didn't really raise this as an objection in this particular instance because, as I said, I'm not particularly concerned with this witness. I raised it because it occurred once or twice today and I just wanted to get clear for the benefit of us, Defence, and the Court what the practice would be in this trial so that we could be consistent and that if it's going to be one way, we'll do it that way; if it's going to be the other way, we'll do it that way, but just to get guidance from the Court on that issue. It's in that spirit that I have raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you, Mr. Whiting. First of all, the witness -- the person who is supposed to have made the statement is a witness who has testified in this court. Okay. And the question is put clearly: "Witness Dzakula appeared before this Court, who is from this area and who explained that on that day ..." and then it goes on. Have you heard about that? There are two distinctions here. One, it's a witness that has testified here, and you say if that is the case, you would concede. Two, the question is not can you comment on that and therefore inviting the witness to comment on the credibility of other witnesses. The question is, have you heard of the statement that Mr. Dzakula has said to have made? Either he has or he has not. And he answered very clearly: From the media, yes. There is no invitation to comment on -- on the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know how far the Court wants to take this, but I think oftentimes that question, however it's phrased, inevitably leads to the witness to -- because -- because the witness has been confronted with this other person, inevitably leads the witness to say, "Well, that witness is not telling the truth," or "That witness is a liar," or whatever. So even though the question is not put necessarily in that specific way, that's where we end up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid the witness must answer the question as put to him. And if, if there should arise a situation where the witness is invited to comment, let's deal with it at that stage, but at this stage I don't think that the Bench sees a basis for the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We stopped at Pakrac, Mr. Babic, so it is not in dispute that this was an event in early May 1991, and this was an armed conflict. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that in mid-March 1991, the Presidency of Yugoslavia did not impose a state of emergency. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Federal Secretariat for National Defence made a proposal for the imposition of a state of emergency with the explanation that the civil war in Yugoslavia had already started?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the events near the Plitvice lake on the 31st of March, 1991, when there was a clash between the Croatian police and the Serbian police officers. Do you know whether this event occurred on some sort of holiday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was Easter. I don't know according to which calendar, the new one or the old one or according to both calendars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the events at Plitvice lakes, did you confirm that the JNA intervened there also and separated the sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the main SDS board immediately before the incident at the Plitvice lakes took the position to negotiate with the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the conclusion was. I didn't attend that meeting. If you're thinking of the meeting at Obrovac, which was also attended by -- no. No, I didn't attend that meeting. I was thinking. I remember that after that meeting Goran Hadzic was at Plitvice and he was arrested by the Croatian police. That's the only thing that I remember in relation to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We heard the testimony of a witness here about that, so I'm not going to put that specific question to you. But I will ask you if you know whether with the mediation and engagement of the Serbian side and the SDS Goran Hadzic was released from prison but that he was severely beaten, however.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly who mediated, but I know that there was some mediation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in relation to these negotiations to release Goran Hadzic the Serb side, as an act of goodwill, adopted the decision to remove the barricades at Borovo Selo before the conflict on the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 1st of April, 1991, the SAO Krajina government adopted a number of decisions. Could you please remind us, which were the decisions adopted on the 1st of April, 1991, relating to the events at Plitvice lakes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to join SAO Krajina to Serbia. That was one of the decisions. The second decision was sent to the federal organs regarding the engagement of the JNA searching or sweeping the terrain and also the activities of the Red Cross to find the missing, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second decision of the 1st of April, did you request the help and protection of the federal organs in relation to the activities of the -- or the actions of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina have constitutional and legal authority to make the decision to join the territory or a part of the territory to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a political provocation. As to if it had the constitutional right to do that or not is something that can be discussed, but this was a political provocation in relation to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how Serbia acted to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know how Slobodan Milosevic reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I asked you if you knew what the reaction of the Republic of Serbia was. My question was quite specific. We will come to Slobodan Milosevic. Now I'm asking you about Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, tell me who you were thinking of when you say "Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia on the 2nd of April adopted a decision supporting the political struggle of the Serbian people in Krajina but did not accept the decision -- that was the gist of the decision, but did not accept the decision on joining Serbia, which you described as a political provocation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in response to your requests for technical assistance to the Krajina SUP, the MUP of Serbia sent some people and that you saw them at the Golubic centre. Is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about how I expected something else. These were expert cadres for the Secretariat for Internal Affairs and not what happened at Golubic. What happened at Golubic was something different from what I expected to be in the form of technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what kind of technical cadre and what kind of technical assistance did you expect from the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected specialist cadres who were legal experts and criminal law experts who would organise the work in the ministry, in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did you make an oral or written request in this sense to the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the request that you cited and I said that this was the result of the promise by Milosevic that he would provide help in cadres for the secretariat in the way that I requested it from him and in the way that I explained it to him. That was the sort of assistance in staff that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you state that in April you went to the Golubic centre and you saw that special police forces were being trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this training in May. In April I saw Milan Martic. There was no training. It was only Martic there, Captain Dragan, and some other people. The centre was not providing training at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Babic. I made a mistake. You corrected me. Yes, that is exactly what you said. Thank you. So in May you went to Golubic, and you said that you saw Nikola Amanovic there; is that correct? He was handling all the files.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the administration, the files. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain that these were groups of people who were arriving from different municipalities in Krajina, who had specialist training, and this was something that was shown to you at that time, and also that these people were undergoing ideological training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain that this ideological training was explained to you in such a way that the people who were attending this special course for the police were trained not to act in accordance with instructions by the parties but only to adhere to the interest of the state, that their actions should be guided by the interests of the state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the month of May, 1991, two referendums were held; and can you tell us briefly what they were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of May, a referendum was held in Croatia and another referendum was held in the SAO Krajina about the status, the state status of Croatia; i.e., the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document number 62 from the 65 ter documents on our monitors. This is a decision to appoint a central commission for carrying out the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears on the monitor, Mr. Babic, I'm going to put a question to you. Do you remember that the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, at its first session held on the 30th of April, 1991, passed a decision on the appointment of central commission? It's on the monitor right now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is the "Central Commission for carrying out the referendum in the territory of the SAO Krajina for annexing SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and to have Krajina remain in Yugoslavia with Serbia, Montenegro, and others who wish to preserve Yugoslavia." Was that the name of the commission, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the corrected name of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Above this text where it says "Decision," is it stated on the basis of what this decision is being passed, and does that say that it's being passed, this decision, on the basis of the law on referendum and other forms of personal expressions of views and the decision on organising a referendum for the annexation of the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I wrong if I state that the first decision of the referendum of the Serbs in Krajina was the decision to annex the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and that this decision in effect modified that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or, rather, as for the referendum question itself, it was changed ultimately, the question itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I'm -- am I right if I state that the first question was supposed to be as follows: "Are you in favour of the annexation of the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia on the 30th of April?" Do you agree that you -- it should read as follows: "Are you in favour of the annexation of the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and that Krajina remains in Yugoslavia together with Serbia, Montenegro, and others who wish to preserve Yugoslavia?"

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have another document displayed on the monitor. The number is 958, 958 from the 65 ter list of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document appears on our monitors, Mr. Babic, I'm going to tell you that this is a record dated the 8th of May, 1991, from the regional meeting of the SDS held that day in Smrtici. Do you recall the content of this document now that you've heard its name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later I heard about some meeting, but it was later. I don't know where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the rest of the text? Can we see paragraph under I? Can we see that on the monitor, please. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does this paragraph I one say, that this meeting in Smrtici was opened by Dzakula, that he gave the floor to Dusan Ecimovic who said that they were in Belgrade and saw Raskovic and Milosevic with Dusan Pekic. They attended a meeting with the opposition that was outside the parliament, and as far as talks with Milosevic were concerned, Milosevic was angry at the Krajina because it reached decisions without consulting him. So he suggests that if a referendum is indeed held on the 12th of May, then the ballot has to read as follows: "For remaining in Yugoslavia, not Serbia." Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not a document from the organisation where I was, but, yes, that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, before we forget, are these two documents that you've just referred to, are they already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first document has already been exhibited, whereas the other one is one that I will tender. I would like to have it admitted as a Defence exhibit. Or do you think I should tender it straight away? I thought that I should put the contents to the witness first, but then I can tender it straight away. So this is a record of the meeting held in Smrtici. Could it please be a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you say the first one was already tendered. It's already an exhibit. I'm being advised it is not an exhibit yet, the first one, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then my information is wrong. So the first document, the decision of the appointment of the Central Commission, could that please be exhibited as a Defence exhibit. I do thank you for your assistance and for having cautioned me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Okay. That document, what was it, the decision on the referendum, it's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now this one that's on the screen, Mr. Milovancevic, are you also tendering that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it will be admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have II on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. The interpreters could not hear the ERN number. But anyway, the page is II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? Please speak into the microphone because the interpreters could not hear some of the statements you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So could we please have page 2, and could we see the very beginning of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, here we have paragraph II stating that Dzakula is presenting the conversation with Sloba. His basic request is that we no longer clash with the MUP but that we leave them clash with the army and that the army can deal with the NDH without any problems. And the last paragraph under number II says: "At the same time, he supported direct talks with the leadership, at least to see what they think." Is that what this paragraph number II says, Mr. Dzakula [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've probably confused me with Dzakula, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Babic. It was a slip of the tongue. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it on the screen now, what you've been reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the top of page 2 again. Can we see it on the monitors? Yes, that's right, so we see number II, what is written under number II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is the text that I referred to just now actually written in paragraph II?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] III. Could we have the rest of the text on the monitor. So could the III be sort of around the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The referendum on the 19th of May, 1991, should be boycotted, and as for the one on the 12th of May, 1991, only Pakrac and Okucani." Is that what is written here in that sentence, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This referendum on the 19th of May, 1991, is that the referendum that was scheduled by the Croatian leadership for the independence of Croatia, and the other one is the Serb referendum that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first one is the Croatian one, the second one is the Serb one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Underneath this sentence comes the next paragraph: "I propose that attempts be made to talk to Knin and Babic so that the referendum of the 12th of May, 1991, be postponed due to the political situation, because some are voting one way, others another way, and third ones in yet another way which is the worst of all." After two omitted sentences, the conclusion is: "However, there are still many remaining ambiguities. What happens if Knin continues to support the wording that reads as 'for Serbia' and the rest 'for Yugoslavia'? Then there's quite a bit of disagreement remaining. After that, Sasic explained very extensively and in professional terms why my proposal to do one's best to postpone the referendum -- or, rather, I stand corrected. As for my proposal to make an attempt to postpone the referendum because it has no legal grounds, most of the Serbs would remain outside the Krajina, and this would mean a knife in the back of Serbia." Is that the text contained in paragraph III, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The participants in this meeting held in Smrtici on the 8th of May, are they talking about the referendum and how the referendum question should read? So what should be the referendum question for the Serbs? Are they voting in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia or being annexed to Serbia? Is that the dilemma that's referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm reading this, and on the basis of these few sentences I can sort of make assumptions, but it's clear to me that they're talking about the referendum and the formulation of the referendum question and the initiative about the referendum question in Knin and some other initiative that others have. If I have managed to understand what this means. This is a regional SDS committee from Slavonia, not from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the very outset, at the very beginning of this document, what did the participants in the meeting state; that the President of Serbia, Milosevic, is in favour of the following referendum question: Are you in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia? rather than it being phrased as: Are you in favour of being annexed to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is your question, whether that's written in this text or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the text now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the very beginning of the text, page 1. Could we see the top of page 1 on the monitor. Could we have it up just a little bit so that we can see the first paragraph of the text. That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this second paragraph, is it being stated that according to Milosevic the ballot should read "in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia," not "in favour of being annexed to Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the referendum held in the Krajina on the 12th of May, 1991, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the SAO Krajina, as well as in Pakrac, the referendum commission or committee did not accept the referendum in Pakrac as a referendum. It wasn't implemented by the municipality, so it was just understood to be an expression of the views of the population, whereas the referendum in the Krajina was held on the basis of the law in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the referendum question at the referendum, did it state: "Are you in favour of annexing the Krajina to Serbia or in favour of staying within Yugoslavia for those who wished to preserve it?" We've seen that earlier in this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a slightly abbreviated version of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Krajina leadership did not act in accordance with the proposal of President Milosevic for the question to be, "Are you in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia?" but formulated this broader question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question was done after Milosevic's intervention. The first question was, "Are you in favour of joining the SAO Krajina to Serbia?" After Milosevic's intervention, the question was broadened in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we've seen the appointment or the decision of the Central Commission for the implementation of the referendum, and this was adopted on the 30th of April, 1991. This meeting in Smrtici was held on the 8th of May, 1991, thus eight days after that, and the participants at the meeting claim that Milosevic wanted them to have the question state: "Are you in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia?" and not the way it was formulated here. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I don't know exactly what they talked about and discussed with Milosevic over there in Slavonia. I already talked about what I know about Milosevic's position. He was strongly against declaring the annexation of Krajina to Serbia, and he even threatened me, in a way, that this must not be done in that way and that the link with Serbia must not be presented in that way, but it had to be presented as whether there was a wish to remain within Yugoslavia. Why I presented it that way was to provoke him to explain precisely to the public what his actual position was, because like I say, he stated one thing in public and did something else in secret. So the reason why I did that was to force him to come out publicly and state whether Krajina should remain within Croatia and seek a solution within Croatia or whether the Krajina should be with Serbia and the others who wished to remain in Yugoslavia. I wanted him to explain that to the public because he was explaining to me that Krajina or the territories inhabited by Serbs need to remain together with Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, while at the same time he was negotiating with Tudjman to give Krajina and a part of Bosnia to Croatia. So after all this that I learned after the meeting with Milosevic and after the meetings with Tudjman at Karadjordjevic, there was this political provocation to make him come out specifically with his position before the Serbian public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. I understand. And was a referendum held in Croatia on the 19th of May, 1991, and what was its result?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia mostly came out in favour of an independent Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the leadership of Croatia and Slovenia, did they on the 25th of June, 1991, adopt a decision on the secession from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was called the declaration on independence. Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the declarations of independence were acts of secession on the part of those two republics from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secession or disassociation, depending on who interpreted it in which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Federal Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, at the request of the Federal Executive Council, declared these acts by Slovenia and Croatia as unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the details, but I know that there was an intervention in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that decision by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia on the non-constitutionality of the secession acts was delivered to the European authorities and Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Babic, that -- do you know, Mr. Babic, who was in the Presidency in Yugoslavia in May and June 1991? Let me put the specific question to you. From Slovenia it was Drnovsek, from Serbia Jovic, from Croatia Mesic, from Macedonia Vasil Tupurkovski, from Serbia and Montenegro it was Bogic Bogicevic, and from Montenegro it was Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? Mr. Milovancevic has been speaking from the point when he said -- okay. The problem has been solved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The representatives that I mentioned, were they in the Presidency of Yugoslavia in May, June, and July 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when Branko Kostic joined that body. Probably in May. There was a change after March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time the president of the Federal Executive Council was Ante Markovic from -- from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the federal secretary for national defence, Veljko Kadijevic, was also a cadre from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or, rather, I know that he was born in Imotski. He's a Serb from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the federal secretary for foreign affairs in the government of Ante Markovic was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that Budimir Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Cadre from Croatia who was the federal secretary for foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Zdravko Mustac head of the state security service? He was also from Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the problem relating to the election of Stipe Mesic as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia in May and June 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, after the dictate of the European Union, and three ministers - Van den Broek and two other ministers from the European Union - Stjepan Mesic was elected as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, so the president of the state, at the point in time when Croatia, which he represented, had already proclaimed its secession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was mediation in two matters. You used the term "dictate," but as far as I know, there was mediation for Mesic to take over the post of president of Presidency, which he had a right to by rote, and for Croatia and Slovenia to postpone the implementation of their independence for a term of three months and to use that period of time for negotiations to resolve the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Babic, when I say that these are two different things? One matter is the election of Mesic as the head of state, and he was elected after certain problems, whereas a completely different problem is the mediation of the European Community in the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis. There was the Brioni memorandum of the 7th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that this was resolved at the same time, because the crisis relating to the election of Mesic started in May and then in June and July this was being resolved with the assistance of European mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the federal government, headed by Ante Markovic -- and I'm mentioning it as an important fact that he is a cadre from Croatia only because of this ethnic representation. It's a material fact at the moment. Are you familiar with the fact that the federal government sent 2.000 soldiers to Slovenia after Slovenia declared its secession and after it occupied the state borders with Yugoslavia in early July 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether this was in early July, but the JNA did intervene in Slovenia in order to take back the state borders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when we continue your cross-examination, we're going to show you a document demonstrating that this was a decision adopted by the government. So I don't want to spend too much time on that right now. Do you know that there was an attack in Slovenia by the Slovenian Territorial Defence, practically the new Slovenian army, on the JNA and that JNA soldiers were disarmed and cruelly killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a brief war in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the decision by the Presidency of Yugoslavia that the JNA temporarily withdraws from Slovenia until a peaceful settlement of the Yugoslav political crisis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Earlier we mentioned the mediation of the European Community. So again I am asking you, is it true that, thanks to the mediation of the European Community, an agreement was reached between Yugoslavia and all the participants from the Yugoslav entity and members of the European Community that the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on independence and secession be postponed for a period of three months?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware and did you take part in negotiations on the resolution of the conflict in Yugoslavia? Because after Slovenia there was also a conflict in Croatia. Did you take part in negotiations on a cease-fire in Croatia and the concluding of a political agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look on the screen at a 65 ter exhibit, document 1226. This is a letter of the SAO Krajina government of the 5th of September, 1991, sent to the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the letter is on the screen now, could you please look at the letterhead. Is this a letter sent by the government to the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia, and does it say in the left corner that the letter was drafted on the 5th of September, 1991, that it was addressed to the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia, and then these letters in the upper right corner -- could we please scroll down a little bit -- scroll up -- that it was sent to the members of the -- could you please scroll up. That the text is sent to members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia cabinets.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
